canonical_topic: Rolling-window volatility and the outlier drop-off problem
definition: A rolling volatility estimate uses a fixed-length window of recent daily returns (e.g., the trailing year), adding one new observation and dropping the oldest each day; volatility is typically computed from the natural-log daily return, ln(price_t/price_t-1).
core_idea: Because a rolling window gives every included observation equal weight, when a large historical price shock ages out of the window the estimated volatility can drop sharply overnight even though nothing unusual happened in current prices.
key_points: Daily return is commonly calculated as the natural log of current price divided by previous price.
In a rolling window, one new observation enters and one leaves each period.
If the observation that leaves was a large outlier, volatility can fall dramatically even with no new market-moving event.
Example given: using a 7-day window around a 9.21% one-day crude oil jump (June 11, 1986), the volatility estimate fell from 3.5% to 2.1% the day after the jump aged out of the 7-day sample.

This matters because instruments like options are highly sensitive to volatility inputs, so a sudden drop in the volatility estimate (unrelated to any real change in market risk) can produce large, hard-to-explain P&L swings in an options portfolio.
relationships: Motivates the use of exponentially weighted volatility as an alternative that avoids the abrupt drop-off effect.
trading_implications: Traders and risk managers should be prepared to explain P&L moves in vol-sensitive instruments that stem purely from an outlier aging out of a rolling-window estimate, not from any actual change in market conditions.
caveats: Interpreting a sudden fall in a rolling-window volatility estimate as evidence that the market has actually become calmer, when it may simply reflect an old outlier leaving the sample.
